summary: Defines SNMP managed objects for managing DS3 and E3 interfaces, which are high-speed digital line types used in telephone and carrier networks. It is a companion to other interface MIB documents.

plainLanguage.summary: Big phone-style data lines need meters to show how healthy they are. This document defines the meters for the larger ones.

subtitle: The SNMP objects for monitoring and configuring DS3 and E3 high-speed digital lines.

tldr.problem: Equipment with DS3 and E3 interfaces needed a common set of SNMP objects so that operators could read line health, error counts and loopback state the same way on every device.
tldr.mechanism: The MIB module defines configuration, current, 15-minute interval and total tables, a far-end group fed by the C-bits, a line status bit map, loopback objects and a line status change notification, all tied to the standard interface table.
tldr.outcome: This is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2496 with small fixes such as a new dsx3M13 line type. It also carries security advice that SET access to many of its objects can interrupt traffic.

facts.label: Severe second threshold
facts.value: 44 or more P-bit or C-bit violations

today: RFC 3896 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2004. It obsoletes RFC 2496, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the DS3/E3 MIB Covers
sections.content:
RFC 3896 defines a piece of the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing DS3 and E3 interfaces through SNMP. It is written in SMIv2 and is a companion to the MIB documents for DS0 (RFC 2494), DS1/E1/DS2/E2 (RFC 3895) and SONET/SDH (RFC 3592) interfaces.

The DS3 definitions are based on ANSI standards (T1.102, T1.107, T1.107a, T1.404) and the E3 definitions on CCITT G.751 and ETSI T/NA(91)18. The design goal is to make common management of all devices with DS3/E3 interfaces possible, so the MIB was aligned closely with the objects that can generally be read from deployed DS3/E3 devices.

It obsoletes RFC 2496. The changes are small: the dsx3FracIfIndex syntax now matches its description range, a reference was added to the Circuit Identifier object, the ifStackTable section was updated, some statistic descriptions were aligned with the near-end and far-end definitions and with RFC 3593, and a new value dsx3M13 was added to dsx3LineType.
sections.plainLanguage: Many companies make big data lines. This document gives them one common list of meters and switches, so an operator can read any of them the same way.

sections.title: Interface Table, Stacking and Channels
sections.content:
A DS3/E3 line appears in the standard interface table with ifType ds3(30). Only the ifGeneralInformationGroup needs to be supported. ifSpeed is 44736000 for DS3 and 34368000 for E3, ifHighSpeed is 45 or 34 megabits per second, and ifPhysAddress carries the Circuit Identifier, or a zero-length octet string if none is assigned.

The old dsx3IfIndex object is deprecated. dsx3LineIndex should now equal ifIndex, and the ifStackTable is used to show which DS3 is attached to which in the proxy case, for example a router and a shelf of CSUs. The RFC says this is not meant to model TDM connections in general. An SNMP proxy here is an application that answers SNMP messages on behalf of the devices that really hold the interfaces, and may therefore miss some statistics.

Channelization is controlled by dsx3Channelization. Setting it to enabledDs1 makes the agent create 28 DS1 interface entries, and each DS1 can in turn carry 24 DS0s. Setting it to enabledDs2 creates 7 DS2 entries, each holding 4 DS1s. The mapping from parent to child interfaces is recorded in the channel mapping tables of the DS1 and DS0 MIBs, and setting the object to disabled destroys the channel entries.
sections.plainLanguage: A big pipe can be split into smaller pipes. The MIB says how to list the big pipe and the little ones, and how to show which little pipes belong to which big one.

sections.title: Loopbacks
sections.content:
A loopback sends a signal back where it came from, for testing. The object dsx3LoopbackConfig is the loopback a manager wants. A manager can request dsx3NoLoop, dsx3PayloadLoop (with ESF framing), dsx3LineLoop, dsx3InwardLoop or dsx3DualLoop (line plus inward). The far end can also request line loopback and payload loopback (with ESF framing), or turn them off, through the FDL channel with ESF or in-band with D4.

The read-only dsx3LoopbackStatus is a bit map of what is actually active, including whether each loopback came from the near end or the far end. It was introduced so that the config object keeps meaning the desired state while the status object shows the real one.

The rules are: the far end cannot undo a loopback set by a manager, and a manager can undo one set by the far end. Only a line loopback and an inward loopback can exist at the same time. A far-end line loopback request adds to an existing inward loopback set by a manager, and if the far end later sends NoLoopback, the inward loopback stays in place.
sections.plainLanguage: A loopback is like shouting into a canyon to hear your own echo, to check that the line works. The person in charge of the line can always turn off the echo, but the far end cannot turn off the one the boss started.

sections.title: The Object Tables
sections.content:
Section 3 holds the module itself, named ds3 under transmission 30. It has a near-end group of four tables (Configuration, Current, Interval, Total) and a far-end group of four tables, plus a fractional table that is deprecated, a trap and conformance statements.

The configuration table holds objects such as dsx3LineType (values include dsx3M23, dsx3SYNTRAN, dsx3CbitParity, dsx3ClearChannel, e3Framed, e3Plcp and the new dsx3M13), dsx3LineCoding (dsx3B3ZS or e3HDB3), dsx3SendCode, dsx3CircuitIdentifier (up to 255 characters), dsx3TransmitClockSource (loopTiming, localTiming or throughTiming), dsx3LineLength (0 to 64000 meters) and dsx3Ds1ForRemoteLoop (0 to 29, where 0 means none and 29 means all).

dsx3LineStatus is a bit map that can report several failures and a loopback at once. dsx3NoAlarm is set if and only if no other flag is set. The far-end table reports configuration received in the C-bits from the remote end, including equipment, location, frame, unit and facility ID codes carried in the Path Identification Message.

The one notification, dsx3LineStatusChange, is sent when an instance of dsx3LineStatus changes and carries dsx3LineStatus and dsx3LineStatusLastChange. It can be used by a management station to trigger polls. It is controlled by dsx3LineStatusChangeTrapEnable, whose default is disabled. When the change also causes a lower-level (DS1) change, no traps for the lower level are sent.
sections.plainLanguage: The tables are like a dashboard: one panel for settings, one for the current count of troubles, one for each recent 15-minute stretch, and one for the whole day. A bell rings if something changes.

sections.title: Counting Errors and Unavailable Time
sections.content:
The error terms follow the draft that became ANSI T1.231, but if the RFC and T1.231 differ, the implementer should follow the RFC. Error events include bipolar violations (BPV), excessive zeros (EXZ), line coding violations (LCV, the count of BPVs plus EXZs), P-bit coding violations (PCV) and C-bit coding violations (CCV).

Performance parameters are accumulated in fifteen-minute intervals, and an agent keeps up to 96 intervals (24 hours), plus a rolling 24-hour total. The counters are Gauge32 types because they can decrease. The per-interval counters are Line Errored Seconds, P-bit Errored and Severely Errored Seconds, C-bit Errored and Severely Errored Seconds (C-bit Parity and SYNTRAN only), Severely Errored Framing Seconds and Unavailable Seconds. A P-bit or C-bit severely errored second has 44 or more violations, or an out-of-frame defect, or an incoming AIS.

Unavailable Seconds (UAS) are the subtle part. The interface becomes unavailable at the onset of 10 contiguous PSESs or of a failure, and becomes available again after 10 contiguous seconds with no PSESs, subject to failure clearing time. While it is unavailable, only UAS is incremented. This means an agent cannot know for 10 seconds whether a given second counts as available time. An agent that updates in real time must therefore adjust counts retroactively by 10, which can even change the previous interval across a 900-second window boundary. Alternatively the agent may delay updates by 10 seconds, sketched in Appendix B as a 10-element delay line. A linkDown trap is sent only after the unavailable state is certain, but it carries the time of the first UAS, ten seconds earlier.
sections.plainLanguage: Every 15 minutes the line gets a report card with counts of bad seconds. The tricky part is that you only know a stretch of seconds was bad after ten more seconds pass, so the report card is sometimes corrected.

sections.title: Defects and Failure States
sections.content:
The RFC defines the conditions a DS3 or E3 line can report. A Loss of Signal (LOS) defect for DS3 is declared on 175 plus or minus 75 contiguous pulse positions with no pulses, and ends on an average pulse density of at least 33% over that span. An Out of Frame (OOF) defect for DS3 is detected when three or more errors occur in sixteen or fewer consecutive F-bits, and a Loss of Frame failure is declared when OOF lasts 2 to 10 seconds. For E3, OOF is four consecutive frame alignment signals received incorrectly, and alignment returns on three consecutive correct signals.

The Alarm Indication Signal (AIS) for DS3 is a framed signal with an alternating 1010 pattern and stuck stuffing; for E3 it is nominally a continuous stream of ones, to be detected and acted on within 1 ms. A Remote Alarm Indication, also called yellow, is reported when the far end signals a problem, for example through the two X-bits in an M-frame set to zero. An incoming failure is declared when LOS, OOF or AIS persists for at least 2 to 10 seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: When a line goes quiet, scrambled, or starts shouting a constant alarm, the MIB has a name for each problem. A problem only counts as a real failure if it keeps going for a few seconds.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Many objects in this MIB are read-write and can harm networks if set wrongly or without protection. Setting dsx3LineType, dsx3LineCoding, dsx3SendCode, dsx3LoopbackConfig, dsx3TransmitClockSource, dsx3LineLength, dsx3Channelization or dsx3Ds1ForRemoteLoop to incorrect values may interrupt traffic. For example, both ends must use the same dsx3LineType for traffic to flow, and some loopbacks stop transmission.

Wrong far-end ID codes cause the remote end to receive an incorrect Path Identification message. A wrong dsx3CircuitIdentifier does not harm traffic but can make troubleshooting harder, and dsx3LineStatusChangeTrapEnable can raise the number of traps a management station receives.

Readable objects can also be sensitive because they reveal performance and some configuration. SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security, so the RFC RECOMMENDS SNMPv3 with cryptographic authentication and privacy, and says deploying earlier versions is NOT RECOMMENDED. Operators must make sure only legitimate principals can GET or SET the objects.
sections.plainLanguage: Some switches on the dashboard can turn off the whole pipe if flipped wrongly. So only trusted people should be allowed to touch them, and messages to the machine should be protected.
